notes: The overview reports no dependency cycles and no orphan modules, so neither is discussed.

claims.text: The `kvstore` crate is the library: it declares three modules — api, cache and storage — and re-exports `handle_request`, `Response`, `Cache` and `FileStore` as its public surface.

The `kvstore-cli` crate is a single-file binary described as a "Minimal CLI exercising the kvstore API": it builds a 64-entry cache, then feeds each command-line argument through `handle_request` and prints the debug form of the response.

The protocol is a colon-delimited wire string documented as `verb:arg[:arg]`, with exactly two recognised verbs — `get`, which looks a key up in the cache, and `put`, which stores one — and anything else answered with `Response::Error("unknown verb")`.
Neither crate has a third-party dependency: the library's `[dependencies]` table is empty and the CLI depends only on the library by path.

The levels track a straightforward layering inside the library: cache.rs sits at level 0 and imports nothing from the crate, api.rs at level 1 imports only the cache, and lib.rs at level 3 sits on top of all three modules.
storage.rs sits above api.rs rather than below it: its only intra-crate import is `crate::api::Response`, which it uses to phrase a read outcome as an API response in `status_response`.
The two crates are joined only at the CLI: kvstore-cli imports the library's `handle_request` and `Cache` and nothing else, so the whole library-to-binary contract is those two names.

cache.rs holds most of the crate's declared surface — 13 of its 14 symbols are public — because it defines two independent public types, `Cache` and `SharedCounter`, each with its own inherent methods.
Start at kvstore-cli/src/main.rs: it is twelve lines and shows the whole runtime shape — construct a cache, hand each argument string to `handle_request`, print the `Response`.
Read api.rs second: `handle_request` is the only function the CLI calls, and its match over the verb is the complete definition of what the store can be asked to do.

lib.rs is worth reading for orientation rather than logic: it contains one item beyond the module declarations and re-exports, and its header comment is the only stated description of what the crate is.

storage.rs can be read last and largely on its own — nothing in api.rs, cache.rs or the CLI calls into it, and its only tie to the rest of the crate is the `Response` enum it returns from `status_response`.
cache.rs is the foundation — three modules depend on it and it depends on nothing in the crate — so its storage semantics are felt by every path that stores or retrieves a value.

`Cache::put` and `Cache::get` are the two methods the request layer actually calls, and both take `&mut self` — which is why the CLI has to hold a mutable cache and pass it into every request, and why a read is not a shared operation here.

`Response` in api.rs is the shared vocabulary of the project: it is what `handle_request` returns, what the CLI prints, and what storage.rs imports from api.rs, so changing its variants touches all three files.

Eviction is concentrated in one place: `Cache::put` is the only caller of `evict_oldest` inside the crate, but `evict_oldest` is `pub`, so its behaviour is also part of the library's external contract.

The crate doc describes "an in-memory cache in front of a file-backed store", but no code wires the two together: `handle_request` reaches only the cache, and `FileStore` is constructed nowhere in the workspace. The file-backed half is present as a type, not as a layer under the cache.

"LRU" means something weaker here than usual: cache.rs calls itself "LRU-ish", `get` does not touch the `order` queue, and `put` pushes unconditionally to the back — so eviction follows insertion order, not recency of use.
The `hits` counter on `Cache` is incremented on every successful `get` but is never read anywhere in the crate, and there is no accessor for it among the type's public methods.

`SharedCounter` lives in cache.rs but is unrelated to `Cache`: it is a mutex-guarded map, it is not re-exported from lib.rs alongside `Cache`, and nothing else in either crate refers to it — it is reachable only as `kvstore::cache::SharedCounter`.

`put` and `get` are not written to the same standard of care despite arriving from the same untrusted wire string: the `get` branch matches on the missing-argument case, while the `put` branch unwraps a missing key, a missing TTL field and a failed TTL parse.
A `put` does not store the caller's value — it stores the string `"ttl={ttl_secs}"` derived from the third field, so the cache's values are formatted TTL text rather than user data.
storage.rs holds the only `unsafe` block in the project — a raw-pointer `read_unaligned` in `magic` that reads four bytes from the front of a caller-supplied slice.

`FileStore` joins the root directory with the raw key, and the doc comment on `read` notes that keys arrive from the wire untrusted; `write` additionally creates any parent directories the joined path implies.

output.summary: kvstore is a two-crate Rust workspace implementing a small bounded key-value store: a `kvstore` library crate whose doc comment describes it as "a small bounded key-value store with an in-memory cache in front of a file-backed store" (kvstore/src/lib.rs:1-2), and a `kvstore-cli` binary that drives it. Requests arrive as colon-delimited wire strings (`verb:arg[:arg]`) and are parsed by `handle_request` in api.rs, which reads and writes a bounded in-memory `Cache` (cache.rs). A separate `FileStore` in storage.rs reads and writes values as files under a root directory and reports outcomes in API terms. The library has no external dependencies at all — its Cargo.toml dependency section is empty — so everything here is standard-library Rust.
